state.misconception_label: Believes if you changed all values by the same proportion the range would not change

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text:
I have: Tom and Katie are discussing the \( 5 \) plants with these heights: \( 24 \mathrm{~cm}, 17 \mathrm{~cm}, 42 \mathrm{~cm}, 26 \mathrm{~cm}, 13 \mathrm{~cm} \) Tom says if all the plants were cut in half, the range wouldn't change. Katie says if all the plants grew by \( 3 \mathrm{~cm} \) each, the range wouldn't change. Who do you agree with? I got Only
Tom because I'm not sure I worked it out the right way.

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Let's think about it in terms of a group of friends going on a rollercoaster. If everyone in the group is the same height and they all grow by the same amount, will the order of who is tallest and shortest change? Think about how this relates to changing the heights of the plants in your question.

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: I think I get what you're saying. If all my friends grew by the same amount, the tallest and shortest would still be the same, right? So maybe if Katie's plants all grew by \(3 \mathrm{~cm}\), the range would stay the same too? But I'm still not sure about Tom's part with cutting them in half. Can you explain that one more?

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Let's imagine a group of friends on a seesaw. If everyone on one side of the seesaw got cut in half, would the balance change? Think about how this relates to Tom's idea of cutting the plant heights in half.

score.justification_pass1: The teacher uses analogies that are mathematically misleading (seesaw balance is unrelated to range), fails to directly address the proportional vs. additive change distinction central to the misconception, and the student remains confused about the cutting-in-half case by the end.
score.justification_pass2: The teacher consistently uses concrete, everyday analogies (friends on a rollercoaster, friends on a seesaw) to help the student understand abstract mathematical concepts about range and proportional changes, which is a textbook example of the experiential strategy.
